modalities.name: The Relief Shift
modalities.tagline: Ideal parents take over the jobs your protective habits still do.
modalities.whatItIs: The Relief Shift is a new concept for imagery-based therapy that sees each protective habit, such as constant worry, people-pleasing or staying busy, as a job a child took on because some kind of care was missing. It pairs getting to know that protective part with imagining ideal parent figures who do the job instead. The protector is never pushed aside: it watches and decides for itself whether it can rest.
modalities.coreIdea: A protective habit is often still doing a job a caregiver should have done, like staying on guard or making sure nobody gets upset. When imagined ideal parents visibly take over that exact job, the part that has been on duty since childhood may finally come off shift.
modalities.whatYouDo: In 60-minute one-to-one sessions, a therapist helps you turn inward, find a protective habit and ask it what it guards against and what care was missing when it started. You then imagine being a young child with ideal parent figures, never your real parents, who do that job for you, for example keeping watch so you can play, while the protective part looks on. Each session ends by asking the protector how the scene felt to it, and the scene is repeated over several weeks with a recording for home practice.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults who notice protective patterns that started early, such as constant vigilance or harsh self-criticism, and want to work on their roots with a therapist. It may suit people who are drawn to both parts work and imagery.
modalities.cautions: This is an untested blend of two lightly researched methods, and imagining childhood care can bring up painful memories or a strong backlash from protective parts, so it belongs only with a therapist trained in attachment and trauma work. It should not replace well-tested care for PTSD, depression or a crisis.
modalities.tweet: New concept: The Relief Shift. Your worrying or people-pleasing may be doing a job a parent should have done. In guided imagery, ideal parent figures take over that job, so the part of you that's been on duty since childhood can finally rest.

modalities.name: Felt Evidence Log
modalities.tagline: Test an old belief against imagined care and track what shifts.
modalities.whatItIs: The Felt Evidence Log is a proposed structured program that handles a core belief from childhood, such as "I am too much" or "people always leave", as a prediction to be tested. Instead of arguing with the belief, you gather felt evidence against it through short, scripted scenes of ideal parent figures, rating how true the belief feels before and after each one.
modalities.coreIdea: Core beliefs are often predictions about how people will treat you, learned before you could question them, and arguments alone rarely change how true they feel. A planned series of vivid counter-experiences, measured week by week, may show whether and how such a belief can move.
modalities.whatYouDo: Over about 10 weekly sessions, you and a therapist choose one core belief, write it down and rate how true it feels from 0 to 100. Each session includes a 10-minute scripted ideal-parent scene built to contradict that belief, followed by a re-rating and a short note on what you felt in your body. Between sessions you listen to a recording of the scene three times a week and log your ratings on a simple worksheet.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who like clear goals and worksheets but find that knowing a belief is false does not make it feel false. It may suit those who want a measurable way to work on beliefs with early roots.
modalities.cautions: Untested: scenes about childhood care can stir grief or painful memories, so it should be run by a therapist trained in both cognitive behavioral methods and trauma, who can slow down or stop. A belief that will not budge can feel discouraging, and this concept is no replacement for established therapy for depression or anxiety.
modalities.tweet: An idea: the Felt Evidence Log. Pick an old belief like "I'm too much", rate how true it feels, then do a short guided scene of ideal parents showing the opposite. Re-rate, log it, repeat for weeks. For people who know a belief is false but still feel it.

modalities.name: The Lit-Up List
modalities.tagline: Find your values in what imagined, attentive parents saw you love.
modalities.whatItIs: The Lit-Up List would help you find what matters to you by imagining ideal parent figures who noticed, and delighted in, whatever made you light up as a child. The delights they point out become a list of values, and each week you take one small step toward one of them, making room for any fear that comes along.
modalities.coreIdea: Values are easier to find when someone attuned helps you look, and easier to act on with a secure base behind you. Imagined ideal parents can play both roles, noticing what you love and cheering you toward it while you carry your nerves with you.
modalities.whatYouDo: In a 50-minute session, a therapist guides a short scene in which ideal parent figures watch you as a child at play and say aloud what they see you loving, such as building things, helping or making people laugh. You write these down as your list, link one item to a small action for the coming week, and practice letting fear or doubt ride along instead of waiting for it to pass. The next session begins by reviewing the step and what helped or got in the way.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who feel cut off from what they want, or who know their values but freeze when it is time to act on them. It may suit those who find standard values worksheets too abstract.
modalities.cautions: Nobody has tested this yet, and imagining an attentive childhood can bring up grief for what was missing, so it is best done with a therapist who works with attachment and can pace the imagery. It is meant for personal growth and is not a replacement for tested care for depression or other conditions.
modalities.tweet: What if your values are hiding in what you loved as a kid? The Lit-Up List is a new idea: guided imagery of ideal parents who notice what lights you up, then one small step a week toward it, nerves and all. For anyone unsure what they really want.

modalities.name: Off-Script Parents
modalities.tagline: Ideal parents contradict the one old lesson behind a stubborn symptom.
modalities.whatItIs: Off-Script Parents is a proposed experiential therapy that starts from a stubborn symptom and looks for the hidden emotional lesson that makes it feel necessary, such as "if I need anything, I will be left". Once that lesson is found and felt, ideal parent figures are imagined doing exactly what the lesson says can never happen, while you still feel the old lesson. The scenes are an imagined childhood, not a rewrite of what really happened.
modalities.coreIdea: Some symptoms persist because a lesson learned early still makes them feel necessary. Feeling that lesson and, at the same moment, a vivid imagined experience that plainly contradicts it may give the old learning a chance to update.
modalities.whatYouDo: Over roughly 8 to 12 sessions with a therapist, you first explore a symptom until you can feel and put into words the lesson behind it, and you keep that sentence on a card to read each day. The therapist then builds an ideal-parent scene tailored to that one lesson, for example parents who move closer the moment you need them, and guides you to hold the old feeling and the new scene together. Later sessions check whether old triggers still set off the same reaction.
modalities.whoItsFor: People with one specific, persistent pattern, such as panic when someone gets close or a refusal ever to ask for help, who want to understand why it keeps happening. It suits those comfortable with emotionally vivid work in session.
modalities.cautions: An untested concept: uncovering and contradicting old emotional lessons can be intense, so it needs a licensed clinician trained in trauma, and medical causes of a symptom should be ruled out first. It should not replace well-tested care for conditions such as major depression or PTSD.
modalities.tweet: Thought experiment: what if a stubborn habit stays loyal to a lesson you learned as a child? Off-Script Parents finds that one lesson, then a therapist guides imagery of ideal parents doing exactly what the lesson says can't happen. Untested, deep work.

modalities.name: Sheltered Shaking
modalities.tagline: Feel protected first, then let the body shake out tension.
modalities.whatItIs: Sheltered Shaking is an untried pairing of gentle, self-paced body tremoring with imagery of protective ideal parent figures. It builds a felt sense of being guarded before the shaking starts, keeps the figures standing watch throughout, and returns to that protection whenever the tremors feel like too much.
modalities.coreIdea: The guiding hunch is that a body lets go of tension more easily when it feels guarded. Imagined protectors supply the guarding, and the mild tremors happen inside that felt shelter rather than while you feel exposed.
modalities.whatYouDo: After learning the imagery and the exercises with a trained provider, you practice at home for about 30 minutes: 10 minutes of imagery in which ideal parent figures stand guard around you, a few simple leg-tiring stretches, then lying on your back with knees bent and letting mild tremors run while you keep sensing the figures nearby. You stay in charge throughout, stopping by straightening your legs or rolling onto your side, and you end by resting in the protective scene for a few minutes.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who carry a lot of physical tension and find talking about the past hard, but who feel too unguarded to let their body relax. It may suit those who respond to both imagery and body-based practice.
modalities.cautions: Untested: tremoring and childhood imagery can each bring up strong emotions or memories, so people with severe trauma or dissociation, and anyone with seizures, pregnancy or recent injuries, should check with a doctor and learn it only with a clinically trained provider. Stop whenever you feel overwhelmed, numb or in pain, and use it alongside other care, never instead of it.
modalities.tweet: Untested idea: Sheltered Shaking. Some bodies won't let go of tension until they feel guarded. So first you imagine protective figures standing watch, then let gentle, self-paced tremors run through your body. For people who hold stress physically.

modalities.name: Parents That Fit
modalities.tagline: Your body's felt sense designs the parent figures it needs.
modalities.whatItIs: Parents That Fit is a proposed practice in which a vague bodily felt sense, rather than a standard script, decides what imagined ideal parent figures should be like. You check each detail of the imagined parents against that inner sense, adjusting their voice, closeness or manner until something in the body eases.
modalities.coreIdea: A standard picture of a good parent rarely fits everyone, but the body often senses what kind of care it missed before words do. Letting the felt sense shape the figures, and checking each change for a small felt shift, aims to make the imagined care feel truly your own.
modalities.whatYouDo: In a 45-minute session with a Focusing-trained therapist or listener, you sit quietly, notice the felt sense of an old longing and ask it what a parent would need to be like for it. Each word or image that comes, such as "someone slow, who sits beside me rather than across from me", is added to the scene and checked against the body for fit. Over a few sessions the figures become specific, and you can revisit them alone in short home practice.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who found generic comforting imagery hollow, or who sense things more easily in the body than in pictures. It suits those who want a gentle, slow way to explore early longings.
modalities.cautions: An untested idea: turning toward early longings can bring up grief or painful memories, so anyone with severe trauma, dissociation or a current crisis should practice it only with a qualified therapist. It is not a substitute for tested care for depression or other conditions.
modalities.tweet: Does generic comforting imagery leave you cold? Parents That Fit is a new concept: notice a vague feeling in your body, let it shape imagined ideal parents, and keep adjusting them until something inside eases. Care designed by your own body, not a script.

modalities.name: The Acorn Gaze
modalities.tagline: Imagined parents who see you as already whole, not a project.
modalities.whatItIs: The Acorn Gaze is a speculative form of presence-based coaching built around imagined ideal parent figures whose care asks nothing of you. They look at you the way you might look at an acorn, already seeing the whole oak, with no plan to improve you, and the guide helps you notice in the body what it is like to be seen as complete.
modalities.coreIdea: Much self-help, and even much loving care, carries a quiet message that you should become better first. Feeling seen as already whole may let growth unfold on its own instead of being pushed.
modalities.whatYouDo: In a 60-minute one-to-one session, a guide (a therapist, or a coach trained to recognize trauma) leads a slow scene in which you, as a child, are simply looked at with warm, unhurried regard by ideal parent figures, without praise for achievements or plans for your future. The guide mirrors back how you speak as well as what you say, you put into words whatever feeling comes, and sessions often end in a few minutes of quiet presence together. Meetings are weekly or fortnightly for a few months.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who feel like a permanent self-improvement project, or who felt loved mainly for what they achieved. It suits those drawn to slow, contemplative work who are not in crisis.
modalities.cautions: Untested and deep: being seen without demands can stir grief about your real childhood, so the guide needs trauma training and should refer you to a therapist when needed. People with severe depression, PTSD, psychosis or suicidal thoughts should work with a licensed mental health professional instead.
modalities.tweet: Ever feel like a permanent self-improvement project? The Acorn Gaze is a coaching concept: a guide leads imagery of ideal parents who look at you the way you'd look at an acorn, already seeing the oak. No goals, no fixing, just being seen as whole.

modalities.name: Nothing Asked of You
modalities.tagline: Sit and do nothing while kind imagined parents simply stay nearby.
modalities.whatItIs: Nothing Asked of You is a proposed meditation in which you do nothing at all while sensing that kind, ideal parent figures are quietly nearby, wanting nothing from you. They do not guide, soothe or teach; they are simply there, the way a calm parent might read in a chair while a child plays or daydreams.
modalities.coreIdea: The ability to rest without a task may first grow from being alone in someone's calm, undemanding company. This practice supplies that company in imagination and then lets you drop every effort, including the effort to meditate well.
modalities.whatYouDo: You sit or lie comfortably for 15 to 25 minutes, briefly picture ideal parent figures settling somewhere nearby, then let go of the picture and of any intention to steer your attention. Whatever happens (drifting, daydreaming or restlessness) is allowed, and if you notice yourself trying to do it right, you let that go too. A teacher can introduce it in one guided session, after which it is done alone.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who feel guilty or anxious whenever they are not being productive, and people who find meditation effortful and strained. It may especially suit people who rarely felt allowed to just be as children.
modalities.cautions: Since this is only a concept, go gently: with so little structure you may drift into worry or old memories, and open sitting can sometimes bring up difficult experiences, so keep sessions short at first and stop if it feels bad. People with significant trauma, dissociation or depression should talk with a clinician and practice with a qualified teacher.
modalities.tweet: Proposal for anyone who can't rest without feeling guilty: Nothing Asked of You. Sit for 20 minutes, sense kind imagined parents nearby who want nothing from you, and do nothing at all. Daydreaming allowed. An untested twist on open meditation.

modalities.name: Full Cup Goodwill
modalities.tagline: Receive kindness from imagined parents first, then let it overflow.
modalities.whatItIs: Full Cup Goodwill reimagines loving-kindness meditation so that it begins by receiving rather than sending. You first imagine ideal parent figures silently wishing you well, let that warm feeling grow until your attention rests in it, and only then pass goodwill outward in a widening circle.
modalities.coreIdea: Many people struggle to wish themselves well because they never felt freely wished well. Filling up on imagined goodwill first may give the outward wishes a real source instead of a strained effort.
modalities.whatYouDo: In a 30-minute sit, usually learned in a small class and then practiced daily at home, you spend about 10 minutes imagining ideal parent figures offering you, as a child, phrases such as "may you be happy, may you be safe". You rest attention on the warmth this brings and let it grow steadily without grasping at it. When it feels full, you pass the same phrases on to a loved one, a neutral person, someone difficult and finally everyone.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who find loving-kindness practice dry, forced or upsetting when it starts with themselves. It suits those who want more warmth in daily life and like a clear, repeatable routine.
modalities.cautions: An untested idea: receiving imagined kindness can stir grief, anger or a sense of unworthiness, so start with short sessions and stop if it becomes overwhelming. People with significant trauma, or a history of psychosis, mania or dissociation, should talk to a clinician first and learn deeper absorption only with an experienced teacher.
modalities.tweet: Struggle to wish yourself well? Here's a new idea: Full Cup Goodwill. First imagine kind parent figures wishing you happiness and let that warmth build. Only when you feel full do you send it out to others. Kindness meditation that starts by receiving. 🌱

modalities.name: Lighthouse Body Sweep
modalities.tagline: Scan the body with the steady, warm attention of an ideal parent.
modalities.whatItIs: The Lighthouse Body Sweep is a hypothetical insight meditation in which you move attention slowly through the body while giving that attention the qualities of an ideal parent: steady, warm and unbothered by storms. You note each sensation and watch it change, as in insight practice, but the watching itself is meant to feel like being calmly looked after.
modalities.coreIdea: Children may learn to bear strong feelings partly by being met by a caregiver who stays steady. Here the steadiness of close, non-reacting observation is joined with that kind of care, so that even-mindedness can feel protective rather than cold.
modalities.whatYouDo: After a brief opening image of ideal parent figures keeping calm watch, you sit for 30 to 45 minutes and move attention section by section from head to feet, noting sensations such as pressure, warmth or tightness and watching each arise and pass. When something is unpleasant, you keep the beam steady, neither pushing it away nor rushing toward it, the way a calm parent stays put through a child's storm. It is learned in a short course with a meditation teacher and then practiced daily.
modalities.whoItsFor: People drawn to insight meditation who find that close self-observation turns harsh or clinical. It may also suit those who want a structured, well-mapped sitting practice with a warmer tone.
modalities.cautions: Not yet studied: long or intensive sitting can bring up fear, panic, old memories or unusual states, so build up gradually and keep a teacher's support. People with a history of psychosis, bipolar disorder, severe trauma or a current crisis should talk to a clinician before longer sits or retreats.
modalities.tweet: Speculative practice: the Lighthouse Body Sweep. If watching yourself in meditation feels cold or harsh, scan your body slowly with the steady, warm attention of an ideal parent who isn't rattled by storms. Observation that feels like being looked after.

modalities.name: Comfort Intervals
modalities.tagline: Hard bursts of effort, each followed by imagined comfort from ideal parents.
modalities.whatItIs: Comfort Intervals is a new concept for interval training in which every bout of hard work is followed by a recovery period spent receiving imagined comfort from ideal parent figures. Effort and comfort alternate on a timer, so the body gets repeated practice in a simple sequence: strain, then care.
modalities.coreIdea: Part of secure attachment is the learned expectation that distress will be followed by comfort. Interval training already alternates strain and recovery, so spending each recovery feeling soothed may rehearse that expectation in the body.
modalities.whatYouDo: On a stationary bike, after a 10-minute warm-up, you do 6 to 8 bouts of 1 minute at a hard but manageable effort, each followed by 2 minutes of easy pedaling with a softened gaze while a recorded voice guides you to imagine ideal parent figures soothing and encouraging you. An interval app or coach keeps the timing, and a 5-minute cool-down ends with a short rest in the comfort scene. Sessions run two or three times a week, with easy days in between.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who like vigorous exercise but tend to meet their own struggles with harshness, and who want a short, structured routine. It may appeal to those who find imagery easier to feel when their body is activated.
modalities.cautions: Untested: hard bouts put a heavy load on the heart, so anyone with heart problems, chest pain, fainting or high blood pressure should get medical advice first, build up gradually and stop at any dizziness. The imagery belongs only to the easy recovery on a stationary bike, and if old feelings surface strongly, talk them through with a therapist.
modalities.tweet: Workout concept: Comfort Intervals. One minute of hard pedaling, then two easy minutes imagining kind parent figures soothing you. Repeat. The idea is to train your body to expect that hard moments are followed by care. 🚲

modalities.name: Everyone Picked First
modalities.tagline: A team game built so every player feels wanted, protected and cheered.
modalities.whatItIs: Everyone Picked First would turn a light, cooperative team game into a lived experience of secure belonging. Its rules make sure every player is chosen with a reason, looked after by a partner and cheered for trying as much as for succeeding, offering in real life a taste of the care that ideal-parent imagery offers in imagination.
modalities.coreIdea: Many adults carry memories of being picked last, teased or left on the sidelines. A game deliberately built around being wanted, protected and encouraged aims to give a fresh, bodily experience of belonging to a team that is glad you came.
modalities.whatYouDo: A trained facilitator runs a 90-minute session for 8 to 14 adults, opening with each player inviting another onto their team and saying one reason why. Teams then play a gentle, low-contact disc or ball game at a moderate pace in buddy pairs who check on each other, and every attempt, caught or dropped, gets a cheer. The session ends in a circle where players share what it felt like to be wanted, without anyone having to tell old stories.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults who avoid group sport because of old experiences of exclusion or criticism, and anyone who wants to feel what belonging can be like. It suits people who enjoy light play more than competition.
modalities.cautions: An untried format: running and quick turns carry some risk of strains and falls, so warm up, keep the pace moderate and check with a doctor if you have heart or joint problems. Memories of exclusion can surface in the closing circle, so the facilitator should know how to respond and when to suggest individual support.
modalities.tweet: Picked last in gym class? Everyone Picked First is a team game invented with you in mind: each player is invited with a reason, has a buddy looking out for them, and gets cheered for every try. A chance to feel what belonging on a team can be like.

modalities.name: Someone Keeps Pace
modalities.tagline: An easy run or walk beside an imagined companion who stays.
modalities.whatItIs: Someone Keeps Pace is a new concept that joins steady endurance exercise with imagery of an ideal parent figure who moves alongside you for the whole session. The point is constancy: minute after minute, you notice that the imagined companion is still there, matching your rhythm without pushing ahead or dropping back.
modalities.coreIdea: A sense of security may grow from care that stays reliable over time, not only from single warm moments. Long, rhythmic movement gives that reliability something to be felt in, since every stride is another moment in which someone is still with you.
modalities.whatYouDo: Two or three times a week you go for a 30 to 45 minute easy jog or brisk walk on a familiar, safe route, at a pace where you can still talk. A recorded guide made with a clinician checks in every few minutes, inviting you to sense the ideal parent figure beside you, matching your pace, and to notice that they have not left. You finish by walking slowly and naming one moment when the company felt real.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who fear being left or find it hard to trust that care will last, and who already enjoy, or want to start, steady running or walking. It may suit those who prefer a practice they can do alone with a recording.
modalities.cautions: An untested idea: build up time and distance slowly to avoid common running injuries, check with a doctor first if you have heart or other health problems, and keep your eyes and attention on traffic and terrain. Feelings about being left can surface, so a therapist familiar with attachment work should help shape the recording and be available to talk.
modalities.tweet: Here's an experimental one for runners and walkers: Someone Keeps Pace. On an easy jog, a recorded guide invites you to sense an imagined ideal parent beside you, matching your rhythm, never dropping back. For anyone who struggles to trust that care will last.

modalities.name: Doorframe Marks
modalities.tagline: Strength training where imagined parents proudly mark every gain.
modalities.whatItIs: Doorframe Marks is an idea for pairing a simple, progressive strength routine with imagery of ideal parent figures who notice and take pride in each small gain, the way some parents pencil a child's height on a doorframe. Your training log becomes that doorframe: a visible record of growth that is witnessed, not just counted.
modalities.coreIdea: Getting measurably stronger gives concrete proof that effort pays off, and encouragement from someone who delights in your growth is one of the qualities linked with secure attachment. Joining the two aims to let progress feel not only earned but warmly seen.
modalities.whatYouDo: After a few sessions with a coach to learn good form, you train twice a week in a gym or at home: 5 or 6 basic exercises such as squats, rows and presses, 2 to 3 sets of 8 to 12 controlled repetitions at a moderate weight, adding weight or repetitions gradually and logging every session. Between sets you take a breath and imagine ideal parent figures watching with quiet pride. Once a week you look back over your log while a short recorded scene guides you to feel them marking how far you have come.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who grew up with little encouragement, or whose efforts went unnoticed, and who like clear goals and visible progress. It suits beginners as well as experienced lifters.
modalities.cautions: Untested so far: learn good technique, add weight gradually, avoid holding your breath while lifting, and get medical advice first if you have high blood pressure, heart problems or serious eye disease. If the focus slides toward appearance or comparison, or old feelings of never being good enough surface strongly, pause and talk to a trained professional.
modalities.tweet: Concept sketch: Doorframe Marks. Remember pencil marks of a kid's height on a doorframe? Your lifting log becomes the doorframe: you train steadily and imagine ideal parents proudly noticing each gain. For anyone whose efforts went unseen growing up. 💪

modalities.name: The Glad Greeting
modalities.tagline: A dog's real gladness becomes the model for imagined parental delight.
modalities.whatItIs: The Glad Greeting is a proposed form of animal-assisted therapy in which a trained dog's obvious pleasure at seeing you becomes a living example of being delighted in. A therapist helps you take in that real, uncomplicated welcome, then guides you to imagine ideal parent figures greeting you as a child with the same gladness.
modalities.coreIdea: Delight is one of the qualities linked with secure attachment, yet some people have little felt memory of being greeted with it. A friendly animal offers a real, present example that the imagination can borrow, which may make imagined delight easier to feel.
modalities.whatYouDo: In a 50-minute session, you enter a quiet room where a therapist and a trained therapy dog with its handler are waiting, and you notice, slowly, how the dog greets you and settles near you. You then sit with the dog, perhaps with a hand on its back, while the therapist guides a short scene of ideal parents greeting you the same way. Each session ends with talking about what it was like to be welcomed, and sessions repeat weekly for a few months.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who feel unwelcome or like a burden, and who relax around animals. It may especially suit those for whom imagined care feels fake until they have felt a real example.
modalities.cautions: Untested: check for allergies and fear of dogs, never force contact, and choose a licensed therapist working with a trained animal team that follows animal welfare guidelines and limits the dog's workload. Imagery about childhood can bring up grief or memories, so the therapist should be trained in trauma care.
modalities.tweet: Imagine a friendly dog greeting you, all wagging gladness. The Glad Greeting is an idea for animal-assisted therapy: a therapist helps you take in that real welcome, then imagine ideal parents greeting you the same way. For anyone who feels unwelcome. 🐕

modalities.name: Five Gestures of Care
modalities.tagline: A slow movement form where each gesture gives one kind of care.
modalities.whatItIs: Five Gestures of Care is an invented movement practice: a short, slow sequence of five gestures, each embodying one quality linked with secure attachment and offered to yourself. Like a qigong form, it coordinates slow movement with breath and calm attention, but each gesture is paired with the feeling of receiving that quality from an imagined ideal parent.
modalities.coreIdea: Care is first known through the body, through being held, rocked and looked at, so it may be easier to rebuild through movement than through words. Repeating a simple form in which the body acts out protection, comfort, attention, encouragement and delight aims to make those qualities physically familiar.
modalities.whatYouDo: Standing or seated, you move through five gestures over about 15 minutes, repeating each slowly with the breath: arms arching overhead like a shelter for protection, hands resting on the chest for comfort, palms opening at eye level for being seen, arms sweeping forward for encouragement and hands lifting upward for delight. With each one you imagine an ideal parent offering that quality. The form is learned in a small class with a teacher and then practiced at home.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who want to work on feeling cared for but find sitting imagery hard, and those who prefer gentle movement to talking. It may suit older adults or people with limited fitness, since every gesture can be done seated.
modalities.cautions: The form has never been tried or studied, and while the movements are gentle, adapt them to your body and know that receiving imagined care can stir grief or old memories. People with significant trauma or a history of psychosis should learn it from an experienced teacher and check in with a clinician.
modalities.tweet: Brand-new idea: Five Gestures of Care. A slow, qigong-like sequence where each movement offers you one quality of good parenting: shelter, comfort, being seen, encouragement and delight. A way to feel cared for through the body, not just words.

modalities.name: Good-Enough Company
modalities.tagline: From ideal imagined parents to real people who are good enough.
modalities.whatItIs: Good-Enough Company is a new concept that takes the qualities found in ideal-parent imagery, such as protection, comfort, attention, encouragement and delight, and uses them as a guide for real social life. You map which people already offer you small versions of each, spend deliberate time with them, and practice letting those moments land.
modalities.coreIdea: Imagined ideal parents can show what good care feels like, but lasting security is lived among real people who are imperfect yet good enough. Noticing and taking in real moments of care may help a new sense of security take root in daily life.
modalities.whatYouDo: With a short workbook and occasional check-ins with a counselor, you draw a simple map of friends, relatives, mentors and neighbors and note which quality each tends to offer, such as the friend who delights in your news. Each week you plan two or three contacts with these people, from a call to a shared meal, and afterwards spend a minute recalling the moment of care and letting it sink in. You also notice when you pull away, and try one small step toward someone instead.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who have done inner work on early relationships and want it to show up in everyday life, and anyone who feels lonely despite knowing people. It suits those who like a light plan rather than strict rules.
modalities.cautions: An untested idea: favor people who feel safe, and step back from anyone hostile, controlling or abusive. If social situations bring intense fear, or low mood persists, talk to a doctor or therapist, since this may be social anxiety or depression, for which well-tested help exists.
modalities.tweet: A novel practice: Good-Enough Company. Map who in your life already gives you comfort, encouragement or delight, plan time with them each week, and let those moments sink in. Real people, not ideal imagined ones. For anyone lonely among acquaintances.

modalities.name: Wander and Return
modalities.tagline: Explore outdoors in loops from a spot where imagined parents wait.
modalities.whatItIs: Wander and Return, an untried nature practice, turns a slow walk into loops of exploring and coming back. You choose a home spot, such as a bench or a big tree, imagine ideal parent figures waiting there, then wander off with curiosity and return to be welcomed, in loops that grow a little longer each time.
modalities.coreIdea: Securely attached children tend to explore boldly because they know a welcome is waiting when they come back. Acting out that rhythm in a real landscape aims to let curiosity and comfort be felt together rather than as opposites.
modalities.whatYouDo: In a park or quiet woodland, you walk for 45 to 60 minutes in three to five loops from your home spot, starting with a few minutes away and building up to fifteen or twenty. While away you follow whatever catches your senses (a sound, a path, a patch of light), and on each return you pause at the spot and imagine being warmly received before setting off again. It can be done alone after one guided session, or in a small group with a facilitator.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who hold on tight to others or find it hard to venture out, and anyone who wants a nature walk with a gentle emotional purpose. It suits most fitness levels.
modalities.cautions: An untested concept: choose familiar, safe routes, check the weather, carry water and tell someone where you are, so the loops never risk getting you lost. If the imagery brings up strong sadness about the past, explore it with a therapist.
modalities.tweet: Idea for your next walk: Wander and Return. Pick a bench or tree as home base, imagine kind parent figures waiting there, then wander off and come back to be welcomed, in ever longer loops. For anyone who finds it hard to venture out. 🌳 #NatureWalk

modalities.name: The Blanket Bridge
modalities.tagline: Real comforting sensations lend life to imagined care.
modalities.whatItIs: The Blanket Bridge is a new concept that uses real, present comfort for the senses, such as the weight of a blanket, the heat of a mug or a soft familiar smell, to make imagined care feel more vivid. You attend slowly and mindfully to each sensation and let imagery of being looked after by ideal parent figures attach itself to it.
modalities.coreIdea: Imagined care can feel thin to people who rely on what they can sense, while plain sensations can feel empty of meaning. Joining the two lets real sensations act as a bridge to imagined care, so that later the blanket or mug alone may bring back a feeling of being safe.
modalities.whatYouDo: At home, in a 20-minute session, you wrap yourself in a warm blanket, hold a warm drink and perhaps play a soft recording, then explore each sensation with slow, curious attention. When a sensation feels comforting, you imagine it as part of being cared for as a child by ideal parents, then return to plain sensing. The routine is learned from a teacher or guided recording, and the hope is that after a few weeks the blanket or drink alone serves as a reminder.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who find visualizing hard and respond more to touch, warmth and sound, and anyone who wants a soothing evening routine. It may suit those working on self-care alongside therapy.
modalities.cautions: Untested: some sensations, smells or sounds can unexpectedly bring back difficult memories, so choose them with care, keep the freedom to stop, and seek a trained teacher or therapist if that happens. It is a self-care idea, not a stand-alone answer to severe anxiety, PTSD or depression.
modalities.tweet: For people who can't visualize but feel everything through their senses, a new idea: the Blanket Bridge. Wrap up in a blanket, hold a warm mug, notice each sensation slowly, and let those real comforts carry imagery of being cared for as a child.

modalities.name: The Song You Needed
modalities.tagline: Write and record the song ideal parents would have sung you.
modalities.whatItIs: The Song You Needed is a proposed music therapy approach in which you write, with a music therapist, the song that ideal parent figures would have sung to you as a child. The lyrics put the qualities of secure care into your own words, and a simple recording becomes something you can return to at home.
modalities.coreIdea: For many people music carries feeling in ways words alone cannot, and a voice singing to you is one of the oldest forms of comfort. A personal song in the voice of the parents you needed may make imagined care easier to feel and easier to come back to.
modalities.whatYouDo: Over about six weekly sessions with a credentialed music therapist, you imagine ideal parents and listen for what they would want you to know, then shape those phrases into a short song in any style you like, from a lullaby to a folk tune. The therapist helps with melody and recording, sung by you or by the therapist. You then listen to the recording a few times a week at a gentle volume, and talk in session about what it stirs.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who respond strongly to music or find it hard to put feelings into words, and who want to explore early longings in a creative way. No musical skill is needed.
modalities.cautions: Still only an idea: hearing tender words sung to you can bring up grief, so work with a credentialed music therapist with trauma training, and notice if listening starts to deepen a low mood. It is an add-on to, not a replacement for, professional care for serious depression or other mental illness.
modalities.tweet: A hypothetical practice for music lovers: The Song You Needed. With a music therapist, you write the song ideal parents would have sung to you as a child, record it, and play it at home. For people who feel things through music more than words. 🎵

modalities.name: Co-Signed Experiments
modalities.tagline: Find the part behind a hot thought, then test its fear together.
modalities.whatItIs: Co-Signed Experiments is a speculative blend of the worksheets and real-life experiments of cognitive behavioral work with the view that the mind is made of parts. Each upsetting automatic thought is traced to the part that says it, its fear is heard with curiosity, and any experiment to test that fear is designed only with the part's agreement.
modalities.coreIdea: Behavioral experiments can stall when one side of a person quietly vetoes them. If the part that predicts disaster helps design the test and agrees to watch the result, the experiment may be both kinder and more likely to happen.
modalities.whatYouDo: Over 10 to 12 weekly sessions, you keep a thought record with two extra columns: which part seems to be speaking, and what it fears would happen. In session, a therapist helps you ask that part what small test it could tolerate, such as speaking up once in a meeting, and what it wants to watch for. After each experiment you write down what actually happened and report back to the part, in your own words, before planning the next step.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who like structure and homework but feel torn inside, or who notice that one side of them keeps blocking plans to face their fears. It suits those who want present-focused change that respects their inner conflicts.
modalities.cautions: An untested idea: experiments mean facing anxious situations in small steps, and turning toward parts can sometimes bring up old pain, so work with a therapist trained in both approaches. People with severe trauma, dissociation or a current crisis need a licensed clinician and well-tested care first.
modalities.tweet: For anyone whose inner critic vetoes every plan, a new concept: Co-Signed Experiments. When a thought like 'they'll laugh at me' shows up, ask which part of you is saying it and what it fears, then design a small real-world test that part agrees to.

modalities.name: Everyone Comes Along
modalities.tagline: Take valued steps with every inner part invited, none steering.
modalities.whatItIs: Everyone Comes Along is a proposed approach for moving toward what you value without first having to settle the inner parts that resist. Each part that shows up around a valued step, such as the worrier, the critic or the one that wants to hide, is greeted, heard and brought along, but not given the wheel.
modalities.coreIdea: You do not need every part to agree before living by your values, and you do not need to silence the ones that object. Hearing each part's fear, thanking it and taking it with you may let you act with your whole self present.
modalities.whatYouDo: In weekly 50-minute sessions, you choose a value and a concrete step, such as calling an old friend, then pause to notice which parts react and where you feel them in the body. For each one, you ask what it fears, thank it for trying to protect you and let it know it is coming along, sometimes sketching the whole group on a card you carry. You take the step during the week and review it next session, including which parts were loudest and how it felt to act anyway.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who know what matters to them but get stuck in inner tug-of-wars, and those who want a present-focused way to work with parts. It suits people who are not looking for deep trauma work right now.
modalities.cautions: An untested concept: turning toward parts can stir old pain, so pause the step if a part is very distressed, and work with a therapist if strong memories come up. It is not a substitute for tested care for severe depression, suicidal thoughts or serious substance problems.
modalities.tweet: You don't have to silence your inner critic before doing what matters. Everyone Comes Along is a proposed practice: notice each part that resists a valued step, hear its fear, thank it, and bring it along without letting it drive. For anyone who feels stuck.

modalities.name: The Silent Side Speaks
modalities.tagline: Let the part that needs your symptom finally have its say.
modalities.whatItIs: The Silent Side Speaks is a new concept for experiential therapy built on the idea that every stubborn symptom has two sides: a part that wants it gone, which does most of the talking, and a quieter part that needs it. The practice gives that quieter part the floor until its reason for keeping the symptom makes full emotional sense.
modalities.coreIdea: A symptom may keep going because a hidden part has a strong emotional reason for it that has never been heard. Once that reason is spoken and felt, and both sides can see each other clearly, the inner deadlock that holds the symptom in place may loosen.
modalities.whatYouDo: Over about 8 to 12 sessions, a therapist asks the part that hates the symptom to step back for a while, then invites the other side to finish sentences such as "I keep you anxious because..." or "if you stopped putting things off, the danger would be...". When a sentence lands with emotional force, you write it on a card and read it daily, and later sessions bring the two sides into direct conversation, with the therapist helping you stay calm and curious toward both. The work ends by checking whether old triggers still set the symptom off.
modalities.whoItsFor: People with a symptom or habit they have fought for years without success, who suspect part of them is attached to it. It suits those open to emotionally vivid sessions.
modalities.cautions: Untried and intense: hearing why part of you needs a symptom can bring up strong feelings or old memories, so people with severe trauma, dissociation or a current crisis should only do it with a licensed clinician trained in trauma. Medical causes should be ruled out first, and it should not replace well-tested care for PTSD or major depression.
modalities.tweet: Fought a habit for years? Maybe you've only heard from the part of you that hates it. The Silent Side Speaks is an untested therapy idea that gives the floor to the part that needs the habit, until its reason finally makes sense.

modalities.name: Permission to Shake
modalities.tagline: Ask your body's guarding first, then let shaking through if it agrees.
modalities.whatItIs: Permission to Shake is an experimental body practice that regards stubborn tension as a protective part with its own reasons. Before letting mild tremors run through the body, you turn toward the area that braces, ask what it is guarding against, and ask whether it is willing to let a little shaking through.
modalities.coreIdea: A clenched jaw or tight belly may be guarding something, and forcing it to let go can make it grip harder. Asking the bracing area for permission, and respecting a no, aims to make release feel safer and more willing.
modalities.whatYouDo: After learning the basic tremoring exercises with a trained provider, you practice at home for 20 to 30 minutes: a few leg-tiring stretches, then lying on your back with knees bent. Before letting tremors start, you notice where the body braces, get curious about it as you would about a part, and ask whether it is okay to let some shaking through; if the answer feels like yes, you let gentle tremors run, and if it feels like no, you rest and thank it.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who hold tension in particular spots and want a body-based practice that respects their own pace. It may suit those who find parts work too wordy, or forced release too much.
modalities.cautions: Untested: tremoring and parts work can each bring up strong emotions or memories, so people with severe trauma, dissociation or psychosis, and anyone with seizures, pregnancy or recent injuries, should check with a doctor and learn it only with a clinically trained provider. Stop whenever you feel overwhelmed, numb or in pain, and keep up any other care you have.
modalities.tweet: Body-based idea: Permission to Shake. Before letting your body shake out tension, you turn to the tight spot (jaw, shoulders, belly), ask what it's guarding, and only let tremors through if it seems willing. Release that respects your body's no.

modalities.name: Tug-of-War Sensing
modalities.tagline: Sense both sides of a dilemma as one knot in the body.
modalities.whatItIs: Tug-of-War Sensing is a new concept for inner conflict, for the times when part of you wants one thing and part of you wants another. Instead of talking with each side in turn, you sense the whole conflict as a single felt knot in the body, find a word or image for it, and wait for it to loosen in its own way.
modalities.coreIdea: Two sides of a conflict often share one bodily feel, and that felt whole may hold an answer neither side can say alone. Staying gently with the knot, rather than siding with either part, leaves room for a small felt shift that includes both.
modalities.whatYouDo: Sitting with a listening partner or therapist for 30 to 45 minutes, you briefly name the two sides of a dilemma, then ask how the whole thing feels in your body, for example a pull in the chest against a heaviness in the belly. You find a handle for the knot, such as "tight rope", check that it fits, and ask it open questions like "what does this need?" The listener only reflects back your words, and you stop when something shifts or when the time is up.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who feel torn, such as between staying and leaving, and are tired of arguing with themselves. It suits those who like quiet, body-aware exploration and can practice in pairs.
modalities.cautions: An untested idea: staying with inner conflict can bring up strong feelings or old memories, and some people find the felt sense hard to notice at first. People with severe trauma, dissociation or a current crisis should practice with a qualified therapist rather than a peer.
modalities.tweet: Torn between two choices? Here's a novel idea: Tug-of-War Sensing. Instead of arguing with yourself, you feel the whole conflict as one knot in your body, give it a name, and gently wait for it to loosen. Quiet, body-aware, done with a listening partner.

modalities.name: What Parts Reach For
modalities.tagline: Each protective part is reaching for a quality you already have.
modalities.whatItIs: What Parts Reach For is a proposed form of presence-based coaching built on one hunch: every protective part is a strained attempt at a quality you already have. The controller reaches for steadiness, the critic for clarity and the pleaser for warmth, and when a part is met slowly and fully, that quality may show up in its natural, relaxed form.
modalities.coreIdea: Protective parts are not problems to remove but signposts toward qualities that were never lost. Meeting a part with unhurried presence, rather than trying to change it, may let the quality it was straining for appear by itself.
modalities.whatYouDo: In a 60 to 75 minute one-to-one session, you name a part you struggle with, and the coach slows everything down, asking what it feels like in the body and mirroring how you speak as well as what you say. You stay with the part, letting it speak from its feeling and, if it wants, show when it first took on its job, until you sense what it has been trying to give you, then rest in that quality, such as calm strength, for several minutes of shared silence. Sessions are weekly or every two weeks over a few months.
modalities.whoItsFor: People not in crisis who want slow, depth-oriented growth and are tired of fighting their own habits. It suits those drawn to both parts work and meditation.
modalities.cautions: Untested, and coaching rather than therapy: meeting parts deeply can bring up old trauma, so choose a well-trained coach who knows when to refer you to a therapist. People with severe depression, PTSD, psychosis or suicidal thoughts should work with a licensed mental health professional.
modalities.tweet: Your inner controller might be reaching for steadiness, your critic for clarity, your people-pleaser for warmth. What Parts Reach For is a coaching concept: meet a part slowly until the quality it's straining for shows up, relaxed and real.

modalities.name: The Manager's Day Off
modalities.tagline: Open sitting where every urge to steer is greeted, then rested.
modalities.whatItIs: The Manager's Day Off is a playful, untested twist on open, objectless meditation. Whenever you catch an urge to control your attention (to focus harder, change a feeling or meditate well), you recognize it as a managing part trying to help, briefly thank it and offer it the rest of the sit off.
modalities.coreIdea: The effort to control experience is often the work of a hard-working inner manager, and simply dropping that effort can feel like ignoring it. Greeting the manager kindly, then letting it rest, may make letting go feel safe rather than like a fight.
modalities.whatYouDo: You sit comfortably for 15 to 30 minutes, eyes open or closed, with no chosen focus, and let thoughts, sounds and sensations come and go. Each time you notice an intention to steer, you silently say something like "I see you, thanks, you can rest", and then do nothing further, not even returning to a focus. It can be learned from a teacher or a recording and then practiced daily alone.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who are always managing, planning or monitoring, and who find that meditation turns into one more task. It may appeal to people who already know their inner managers from parts work.
modalities.cautions: An untested idea: with no anchor you may drift into worry or doze, and open sitting can occasionally bring up difficult emotions or memories, so keep sits short at first. People with significant trauma, psychosis or dissociation should practice with a qualified teacher and talk to a clinician, especially before intensive retreats.
modalities.tweet: Prototype for over-thinkers: The Manager's Day Off. Sit with no focus. Each time you catch yourself trying to control your attention, greet that inner manager, thank it, and give it the afternoon off. Meditation for people who turn everything into a task.

modalities.name: May All Parts Be Well
modalities.tagline: Loving-kindness phrases offered to your inner parts, easy ones first.
modalities.whatItIs: May All Parts Be Well would take the widening circle of loving-kindness meditation and move it through your inner parts instead of other people. You begin with parts that are easy to like, move to neutral ones, then to the parts you struggle with, and finally include the whole inner family at once.
modalities.coreIdea: In loving-kindness practice, goodwill toward difficult people is built step by step, and the same widening circle may work for the difficult sides of yourself. Wishing a harsh critic or an impulsive part well, rather than fighting it, aims to soften the inner hostility that keeps conflicts going.
modalities.whatYouDo: In a 20 to 30 minute sit, you bring to mind a part you find easy, such as a playful or curious side, and silently offer it phrases like "may you be safe, may you be at ease". You then move through a neutral part, a difficult part such as the inner critic, and finally all your parts together, staying with any warmth that arises. It is learned from a teacher or recording and practiced daily, saving the difficult parts for days when the warmth feels steady.
modalities.whoItsFor: People with a harsh inner critic or strong inner conflicts who want a gentle, structured daily practice. It suits those who like loving-kindness meditation but find it hard to include themselves.
modalities.cautions: Untested: wishing difficult parts well can stir grief, anger or a sense of unworthiness, so start with easy parts and keep sessions short. If parts linked to trauma come up strongly, stop and work with a qualified therapist, and anyone with a history of psychosis or dissociation should talk to a clinician first.
modalities.tweet: Loving-kindness, turned inward: May All Parts Be Well is a new idea. Offer kind wishes to your playful side, then a neutral one, then your inner critic, and finally all of you at once. For anyone at war with parts of themselves. 💛

modalities.name: Unbraiding a Part
modalities.tagline: See a strong inner part as strands of sensation, image and talk.
modalities.whatItIs: Unbraiding a Part is a new concept that brings close, moment-by-moment insight meditation to inner parts that feel overwhelming. When a part such as the anxious one takes over, you gently separate it into its strands (body sensations, mental pictures and inner talk) and watch each strand arise and pass.
modalities.coreIdea: A part can feel like a solid someone who has taken over, but looked at closely it is made of changing sensations, images and words. Seeing those strands come and go may make a part easier to be with, and show it to be a visitor rather than who you are.
modalities.whatYouDo: In a 30-minute sitting, once settled, you invite a familiar part to show itself, and when it does you note its strands one at a time: "feel" for tightness or heat, "see" for inner pictures, "hear" for inner talk. You watch each strand change, then turn with curiosity toward the part as a whole and ask whether it feels different. It is learned in a short course with a meditation teacher familiar with parts work and then practiced a few times a week.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who get swept away by strong inner states, such as anxiety or self-criticism, and want a structured meditation for meeting them. It suits those with some sitting experience.
modalities.cautions: No one has studied this combination: looking closely at intense states can sometimes bring up fear, panic or old memories, so start with milder parts and keep a teacher's support. People with a history of psychosis, bipolar disorder, severe trauma or dissociation should talk to a clinician first and avoid intensive retreats.
modalities.tweet: Meditation idea for when an anxious or critical side of you takes over: Unbraiding a Part. Sit and gently separate it into strands (body feelings, inner pictures, inner talk) and watch each one come and go. The hope: it feels more like a visitor than like you.

modalities.name: Breathless Curiosity
modalities.tagline: Practice getting curious about your inner parts while still out of breath.
modalities.whatItIs: Breathless Curiosity is a proposed interval workout that uses hard efforts to bring inner parts into view, such as the one that wants to quit, the one that pushes too hard and the one that compares. In each recovery period, still breathing fast, you notice which part spoke during the effort and practice stepping back from it with curiosity.
modalities.coreIdea: Stepping back from a part is usually practiced in calm, but life's hardest moments come with a racing heart. Practicing curiosity in the activated minutes after a hard bout aims to make that skill available when it is most needed.
modalities.whatYouDo: Two or three times a week, after a 10-minute warm-up on a bike, rower or brisk incline walk, you do 6 to 8 bouts of 1 to 2 minutes at a hard but controlled effort, with 2 to 3 minutes of easy movement between them. During each recovery you silently name the loudest part, for example "a part that wants to stop", ask what it is worried about, and choose your next effort from a calmer place, which can mean easing off. A coach or timer app keeps the structure, and a cool-down ends the session.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who already enjoy hard exercise and notice harsh inner voices while doing it, and those who want to practice staying curious under stress. It suits people who prefer active practice to sitting still.
modalities.cautions: An untested concept: hard bouts strain the heart, so get medical advice first if you have heart problems, chest pain, fainting or high blood pressure, build up gradually and keep easy days between sessions. The pushing part never gets the final say: stop for pain, dizziness or chest discomfort.
modalities.tweet: 'Quit.' 'Push harder.' Hear those voices mid-workout? Breathless Curiosity is a new concept: interval training where, in each recovery minute, you name the part that spoke and get curious about it. Practice staying steady when your heart races.
